# Globalization · c. 1600 CE

## ocean-crossings
### Iberian routes
spot: 2.2, 102.25
view: fit
site: Lisbon · 38.72, -9.14
site: Goa · 15.5, 73.83
site: Malacca · 2.2, 102.25
site: Manila · 14.6, 120.98
area: Atlantic Ocean · 25, -40
area: Indian Ocean · -5, 75

From the 1490s **Portuguese** ships rounded the Cape of Good Hope to Malindi and Calicut, opening a sea route for pepper that competed with the Red Sea. **Castilian** ships crossed the Atlantic from the Canaries to the Caribbean and returned on the westerlies past the Azores, while Portugal reached Brazil.

Gold from **Elmina** and captives from West Africa flowed to Lisbon, and the older Asian networks carried on trading.

**Mauritius**, a watering stop on the way to the Indies, lost the dodo within decades of the Dutch landing of 1598; the last sightings are from the 1660s.

- porcelain-silk: **Porcelain & silk** · China → Indian Ocean ports
- cotton-cloth: **Cotton cloth** · Gujarat → Africa and Southeast Asia
- spices-pepper: **Spices & pepper** · Malacca and Malabar → Egypt and Venice
- bullion: **Silver & gold** · Europe and the Middle East → India

> Lanes follow the winds and currents that made these crossings possible, not the track of any single fleet.

## americas-exchange
### Aztec, Inca and Taíno worlds
spot: -13.5, -72
view: fit
site: Tenochtitlan · 19.43, -99.13
site: Cusco · -13.52, -71.97
site: Potosí · -19.58, -65.75
site: Santa Fe · 35.69, -105.94
site: Buenos Aires · -34.6, -58.38
area: Caribbean Sea · 16, -72

By 1450 CE, **pochteca** merchants carried obsidian, cloth and tribute between Tenochtitlan, the Gulf and Soconusco, while Maya canoes worked the Yucatán coast. The **Qhapaq Ñan** road system moved gold, silver and fine cloth between Quito, Cusco and Chile.

**Taíno** communities exchanged goods across the Greater Antilles and received guanín, a gold-copper alloy, from the mainland. On the Amazon, Santarém pottery and lowland goods moved along the rivers toward the Inca frontier. In the southeast, shell and copper still reached Mississippian towns.

By 1600 the newcomers' roads were pushing outward. The **Camino Real de Tierra Adentro** ran from Mexico City past the silver mines of Zacatecas to Santa Fe (1598); Spanish towns lined the mule road from Potosí to Córdoba and the Paraná down to Buenos Aires (1580); bandeirantes from São Paulo raided inland; and missions and fur posts spread from St Augustine and Quebec.

- obsidian: **Obsidian** · Pachuca → Tenochtitlan and merchant routes
- shell: **Spondylus & shell** · Ecuador → Cusco; Gulf → Mississippian towns
- crops: **Crops** · cacao and canoe cargoes
- metals: **Metals** · Inca tribute; copper; guanín
- feathers: **Feathers, textiles & forest goods** · quetzal, macaws, cloth, coca
- ceramics: **Pottery & river networks** · Taíno islands; Santarém and the Amazon
- frontier: **Settler frontiers** · Spanish and Portuguese roads inland; Florida and St Lawrence outposts

> Roads and sea lanes are simplified; state control of trade varied. Guanín and Amazon links are drawn fainter. Settler roads meant conquest and dispossession for the peoples along them.

## african-networks
### Songhai and the Portuguese
spot: 5.08, -1.35
view: fit
site: Elmina · 5.08, -1.35
site: Gao · 16.27, -0.05
site: Mombasa · -4.05, 39.67
area: Sahara · 22, 10

By 1480 **Songhai**, from Gao, ruled the Niger bend and the caravan trade to Morocco, Tripoli and Cairo. At the same time **Portuguese** ships reached the Atlantic coast: gold from the Akan forest at **Elmina**, pepper and cloth from Benin, and enslaved people from Senegambia and the kingdom of **Kongo**, shipped through Arguin and São Tomé, and by 1600 across the Atlantic to the sugar mills of Brazil and the mines and ports of Spanish America.

On the Indian Ocean the Swahili and Gujarati trade continued, soon to meet the Portuguese as well.

- gold-ivory: **Gold & ivory** · Sahel and Gold Coast → Maghreb and Lisbon
- salt-copper: **Salt & copper** · Sahara → Niger bend
- cloth-beads: **Cloth, brass & beads** · Europe and the Maghreb → Africa
- captives: **Enslaved people** · Sahara, Kongo and Senegambia → Mediterranean, Brazil and Spanish America

> Atlantic lines mark the start of a trade that grew enormously later; the Benin and Senegambia links are drawn fainter.
